episode.title: Cariboo Signals - Arts, Culture & Digital Storytelling
episode.description:
Riley and Casey explore technology and society in rural communities. Today's focus: Arts, Culture & Digital Storytelling.

THIS WEEK WE'RE ASKING: Is it better to be self-sufficient or well-connected?

NEWS ROUNDUP: We break down [Williams Lake Tribune] 8 weeks of live music: Williams Lake Performances in the Park concludes summer and [Williams Lake Tribune] More properties downgraded to all clear as Pear Lake fire near Clinton shows minimal growth, plus 1 more stories, and explore what these developments mean for communities like ours.

RURAL CONNECTIONS: Should arts and cultural institutions prioritize self-sufficient, local-first infrastructure or embrace network-connected platforms to maximize reach and sustainability? Topics include: AI-generated music bans and chart eligibility policies across Australia, Grammy Awards, and proposed US standards, Platform dependency and ownership of master files versus hosting infrastructure vulnerability, Local cultural preservation through digitization and archival challenges for under-resourced institutions, Community partnership models and governance failures in maintaining relationships beyond initial grant cycles, The trade-off between self-sufficient local culture and network-dependent reach for artistic work.

Hosts: Riley (Tech optimist with an engineering background) and Casey (Community-first skeptic of tech promises).

COMMUNITY SPOTLIGHT: Cariboo Chilcotin Partners for Literacy

discussion.central_question: Should arts and cultural institutions prioritize self-sufficient, local-first infrastructure or embrace network-connected platforms to maximize reach and sustainability?
discussion.riley_position: Both approaches have merit depending on ambition and scope; the real solution is building smaller, local-first infrastructure pieces that can plug into larger networks on your own terms, maintaining ownership and control while accessing distribution.
riley_key_evidence: ARIA's updated Charts Code requires substantially human-made music with human performers/songwriting, allowing AI only in supporting production roles
Bandcamp allows artists to keep ownership of master recordings and set their own prices while remaining connected to a platform
Williams Lake's Performances in the Park operated entirely self-sufficiently all summer with local live musicians and didn't require network infrastructure to succeed locally
discussion.casey_position: The fork between self-sufficiency and connectivity is real and unresolvable; staying fully self-sufficient means durability but zero reach beyond the immediate community, while connecting to networks exposes work to platform dependencies, algorithm changes, and the inability to prevent fakes from spreading first.
casey_key_evidence: Josh Fawaz's fully AI-generated Madonna cover reached 48 million Spotify streams before any ban existed, showing the chart policy arrived too late
Vocal cloning is nearly undetectable with current tools, making 'substantially human-made' an honor system that can't stop fakes from reaching audiences first
A Williams Lake Performances concert only reaches as far as the park fence unless recorded and uploaded, requiring the very platform infrastructure that creates the fake-music problem
discussion.resolution: Riley and Casey agreed that the honest answer depends on a community's actual ambitions: local work needs only local infrastructure and can remain self-sufficient, but any work seeking wider reach or archival longevity must accept network dependency. They concluded that communities should decide deliberately upfront whether to archive and distribute performances, rather than discovering this by accident after opportunities are lost.
